item.title: Warren County deputies looking for man wanted on home invasion, domestic violence charges - Darkhorse Press
item.author: Morgan Howard
item.description:
VICKSBURG – The Warren County Sheriff’s Office is asking for the public’s help finding a man wanted on multiple charges.

Deputies said Sims is known to be in the Kings community.

Anyone with information about his whereabouts is asked to contact Lt. Stacy Rollison at 601-636-1761.

Those who wish to remain anonymous and qualify for a cash reward of up to $2,500 may contact Central Mississippi Crime Stoppers.

item.title: Venezuelan man with alleged Tren de Aragua ties sentenced in ATM fraud scheme - Darkhorse Press
item.author: Therese Apel
item.description:
NORTH MISSISSIPPI — A Venezuelan man federal prosecutors say has ties to the international gang Tren de Aragua was sentenced Wednesday in Oxford for his role in a bank fraud conspiracy involving ATM “jackpotting” schemes across Mississippi.

Darrin Daza-Segura, 26, who was living in Dallas as an undocumented immigrant, was sentenced by U.S. District Judge Michael P. Mills to 10 months in federal prison followed by three years of supervised release. He was also ordered to pay $47,250 in restitution.

According to court documents, Daza-Segura will be turned over to U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement custody for removal proceedings following his prison sentence and will not be permitted to re-enter the country without authorization from the Department of Homeland Security.

Federal prosecutors said Daza-Segura and co-defendant Winder Alexander Canelon-Tiapa traveled throughout Mississippi reprogramming ATMs to force machines to dispense large amounts of cash, a crime commonly referred to as “ATM jackpotting.” Authorities said the pair successfully stole approximately $47,000 and attempted to steal more from banks across the state.

Federal authorities nationwide have linked similar “ATM jackpotting” schemes to alleged members of Tren de Aragua, who investigators say use malware to force ATMs to release cash.

U.S. Attorney Scott Leary said the defendants targeted communities in north Mississippi while traveling through the region.

“These Venezuelan gang members have been categorized as terrorists,” Leary said in a statement. “They do not live here but have come to victimize our citizens in North Mississippi.”

Mississippi Attorney General Lynn Fitch said investigators were able to stop a “dangerous TdA gang member from defrauding Mississippians.”

The case was investigated by the Cyber Crime Division of the Mississippi Attorney General’s Office and is being prosecuted by Assistant U.S. Attorney Clayton A. Dabbs.

item.title: Tupelo man charged with felony malicious mischief after display home damaged - Darkhorse Press
item.author: Morgan Howard
item.description:
A Tupelo man was arrested after police said a display home was damaged at Repo Home Center.

According to the Tupelo Police Department, officers responded May 11 to Repo Home Center, located at 2500 S. Gloster St., in reference to a damaged display home.

During the investigation, police identified a suspect. Exzadrin Deshun Levi, 22, of Tupelo, was arrested May 11 and charged with felony malicious mischief.

On May 19, Tupelo Municipal Court Judge Weir ordered Levi held on a $10,000 bond.

The charges will be presented to the Lee County grand jury.

item.title: Rankin County “Goon Squad” victim arrested on firearms charges in Simpson County - Darkhorse Press
item.author: Therese Apel
item.description:
SIMPSON COUNTY — One of the victims in the Rankin County Goon Squad case was arrested Tuesday in Simpson County on firearms-related charges, according to officials.

Eddie Terrell Parker was booked into the Simpson County Jail on May 19 by the Mississippi Highway Patrol, according to Paul Mullins. Mullins said he is still being treated for injuries from a crash.

Mullins said Parker had previously been arrested by the Louisiana State Police in December on multiple charges, including narcotics violations, possession with intent to distribute, felon in possession of a firearm and carrying a concealed weapon.

Authorities have not released additional details about the latest arrest, but we have contacted MHP for more.

Parker was one of two men tortured and abused by former members of the self-described “Goon Squad,” a group of five former Rankin County deputies and a Richland police officer who pleaded guilty in federal court to a series of civil rights violations stemming from the January 2023 raid in Braxton.

item.title: Police investigating attempted shooting, robbery at Southaven Walmart - Darkhorse Press
item.author: Therese Apel
item.description:
SOUTHAVEN — Police are investigating after a robbery and attempted shooting were reported Thursday evening in the parking lot of a Walmart in Southaven.

According to the Southaven Police Department, officers responded around 7:15 p.m. to reports of shots fired in the west parking lot of the store.

Investigators said preliminary information indicates a suspect robbed the victim and then attempted to shoot him before fleeing the area.

No injuries were reported.

Police said responding officers secured the scene and there is no ongoing threat to the business or the public.

The investigation remains active.

item.title: Mississippi Public Safety Summit draws more than 900 first responders, leaders - Darkhorse Press
item.author: Therese Apel
item.description:
FLOWOOD — More than 900 law enforcement officers, firefighters, prosecutors and first responders from across Mississippi gathered this week for the 2026 Mississippi Public Safety Summit, an event state leaders say has become a cornerstone for collaboration, leadership development and public safety training.

The four-day summit, hosted by the Mississippi Department of Public Safety and the Mississippi Attorney General’s Office , began Tuesday night at the Sheraton Flowood/The Refuge with a keynote presentation from motivational speaker and former first responder Travis Howze .

“This was something we knew was needed,” Department of Public Safety Commissioner Sean Tindell told Darkhorse Press during an interview alongside Attorney General Lynn Fitch . “I’m shocked that it has grown this fast.”

The summit, now in its fourth year, began in 2023 as a joint effort between the two agencies. Organizers said attendance has grown steadily each year, from a few hundred attendees at the inaugural event to more than 900 this year.

Fitch said the summit was designed to bring together every level of public safety personnel in one place, something she and Tindell felt was missing from traditional conferences focused only on specific professions or agencies.

“It’s really a unified front,” Fitch said. “Everybody at the end of the day asks, ‘Who do we help? How do we make a difference?’”

Throughout the event, attendees participated in discussions on leadership, mental wellness, communication strategies, digital threats, domestic violence prevention and investigative techniques. Sessions included “Operation Roadkill – Going Undercover with Scott Payne,” “Understanding and Responding to Emerging Digital Threats” with Heather Girton, and “Profiling Serial Killers — Getting Inside the Mind” with Phil Chalmers.

A panel on media relations, “Facing the Press: Confidence, Clarity, and Control,” featured Darkhorse Press publisher Therese Apel alongside Oxford Police Department Public Information Officer Breck Jones and Gulfport Police Department PIO Jason DuCré.

One of the summit’s featured speakers was FBI Co-Deputy Director Andrew Bailey , who participated in a fireside chat Thursday. Fitch noted Bailey previously served as Missouri attorney general before joining FBI Director Kash Patel’s leadership team.

Tindell said one of the summit’s greatest strengths is its ability to foster relationships among local, state and federal agencies before emergencies happen.

“When their backs are against the wall, they don’t care who shows up,” Tindell said. “Whether it’s the fire department, sheriff’s department, police department, state trooper or otherwise. Building those relationships matters.”

Fitch said those relationships often lead to stronger coordination during investigations and emergencies.

“As the relationships are built here, they see one another, they interact with one another, and they’re willing to call on each other,” Fitch said. “That builds trust, and that trust makes us stronger.”

The summit also included the Governor’s Public Safety Awards luncheon, exhibitor halls, networking events and a golf tournament at The Refuge Golf Course.

Both leaders credited the success of the event to the teams behind the scenes organizing the summit and to the agencies statewide that continue supporting it.

item.title: MDWFP, National Park Service to Host Free Youth Fish Camp in June - Darkhorse Press
item.author: Therese Apel
item.description:
JACKSON — The Mississippi Department of Wildlife, Fisheries, and Parks Visitor Education Center at the Bob Tyler Fish Hatchery is partnering with the National Park Service to host a free fish camp for youth ages 10 to 15 on June 10.

The camp will run from 9 a.m. to 3 p.m. and will introduce participants to fishing basics, hatchery operations and the National Park Service Junior Angler Program.

According to MDWFP, campers will learn fish identification, water safety tips and participate in catfish fishing at the hatchery’s Visitor Education Center pond. Youth will also tour the hatchery, meet a National Park Service ranger and learn more about earning the National Park Service Junior Angler Badge.

Fishing equipment and bait will be provided during the event. Participants who complete the full day of activities will receive special items and earn the Junior Angler Badge.

The program is free, but pre-registration is required. Those interested can call the Visitor Education Center at 662-563-8068 or email [email protected] to request a registration form.

The Visitor Education Center is part of the Bob Tyler Fish Hatchery and is located off Interstate 55 at Exit 233 east.

item.title: LEO training board approves new pathway for part-time officers to earn full-time certification - Darkhorse Press
item.author: Therese Apel
item.description:
PEARL — Part-time law enforcement officers in Mississippi will have a new pathway to full-time certification under a rule approved this week by the Board of Law Enforcement Officers Standards and Training.

BLEOST approved Rule 9.5 for filing with the Secretary of State’s Office, establishing an alternative route for currently certified part-time officers to obtain full-time certification through demonstrated competency, training equivalency and sustained service — without completing a traditional full-time academy.

Under the rule, officers who have already completed an approved part-time training program may pursue full-time certification through evaluations conducted by accredited full-time training academies. The rule must complete the formal approval process with the Secretary of State before taking effect. Public Safety Commissioner Sean Tindell said the rule addresses a practical barrier that has kept qualified officers from advancing.

“I’m proud of the work being done to help part-time officers establish full-time certification opportunities for those who want to serve and protect their communities, but may not have the time or financial ability to step away from their other jobs to attend a traditional full-time academy,” Tindell said.

Lee County Sheriff Jim H. Johnson called the rule a meaningful step for agencies struggling to fill full-time positions.

“This is a great change to help our part-time officers achieve full-time status through the proper evaluation and training process that needs to be done to help increase our public safety in local communities across the state,” Johnson said.

BLEOST credited Standards and Training Director Vanderford and Harrison County Sheriff’s Office Captain Hendry with developing and presenting the rule to the board.

item.title: June 18 verdict scheduled in Quinton Tellis murder trial - Darkhorse Press
item.author: Therese Apel
item.description:
MONROE, La. — Closing arguments concluded Thursday in the bench trial of Quinton Tellis, charged with the 2015 murder of Ming Chen “Mandy” Hsiao, with the state painting a portrait of a calculated killer who tortured his victim for her PIN number and the defense arguing the case against their client amounts to little more than supposition built on a foundation of circumstantial evidence.

Judge Larry Jefferson will issue his ruling June 18 at 9 a.m. in Ouachita Parish court.

ADA Holly Jones opened her closing argument by returning to the theme she established at the outset of trial: that Mandy Hsiao was killed by a person devoid of emotion who wanted one thing, her money. She framed the case as a blank canvas filled in fact by fact until the full picture became undeniable.

“When using your reason and common sense, and looking at the existence of all of these facts, such facts will exclude any reasonable hypothesis of the defendant’s innocence,” Jones told Judge Jefferson.

Jones walked the court methodically through three distinct time periods: what investigators knew before Tellis’s first interview on August 11, 2015; what they learned between that interview and his second on August 19th; and what came to light after his arrest. At each stage, she argued, the evidence that emerged contradicted what Tellis had told police. And he had told police, repeatedly and emphatically, that he was telling the truth.

“I’m telling the truth, that I’m going to be straightforward and honest with you. I swear to God, I ain’t got no reason to lie to you. God can kill me right now, and I’m not lying about nothing. That’s on my grandma’s graveyard,” Jones quoted from his August 11th statement, before methodically laying out everything he had omitted from that interview: numerous Chase Bank calls, the fact that he knew Hsiao’s PIN number, the attempt to use Mohammed Mahrous as a money mule, the Vicksburg ATM withdrawals and his assertion that it wasn’t him in the surveillance photos of him, the Exxon receipt found in his home.

Jones saved her sharpest argument for the four phone calls made between 8:16 and 8:18 p.m. on July 29, 2015, two from Mandy’s iPhone and two from Tellis’s Nokia, all to the same Chase automated banking number, all within the same two-minute window. She noted that in six previous calls to Chase in May, Mandy had never once dialed a 1 before the 800 number. She knew she didn’t have to. On July 29th, both calls from her phone included the 1, because, Jones argued, whoever was dialing was reading the number off the back of the debit card, where it is printed with a 1 in front.

“The fact that the four phone calls occurred within the same minute, with the first two being made using Mandy’s cellular phone and the last two being made using the defendant’s cell phone, places Mandy and the defendant together at that point in time without question,” Jones said. “How do we know this? Because on August 8th, when they took all the evidence out of Mandy’s apartment, Mandy’s cell phone was still in the apartment.”

Jones argued that the presence of Mandy’s phone in the apartment on August 8th, combined with its use on the night of July 29th simultaneous with Tellis’s phone, left only one conclusion: he was there. And if he was there and left her alive, Jones said, there was no explaining what came next.

“If he allowed her to live, why in the world would she not immediately pick up the phone and call the police?” Jones said. “Because she was dead. Because he killed her. There is no other reasonable hypothesis.”

Jones addressed the DNA evidence directly, conceding there was none linking Tellis to the scene, but arguing the state of Mandy’s body after 10 days of decomposition in the Louisiana heat would have destroyed whatever was there. She also characterized the Y chromosome found in a rectal swab as not a DNA profile and not evidence of sexual assault, calling it a potential red herring, and noted that 17 people had their DNA tested in connection with the case and none were connected to the scene either.

On the testimony of Eric Hill, Tellis’s wife’s cousin who said Tellis called him from jail and told him to find someone to blame for Mandy’s murder, Jones argued Hill’s knowledge of details that were never made public, including the number and nature of the stab wounds, could only have come from Tellis himself. She acknowledged Hill had told multiple stories but said Detective Duane Cookson’s corroboration of the non-public details was the verification the court needed.

Jones closed by returning to the simplest question in the case. Mandy Hsiao sent a Facebook message at 7:41 p.m. on July 29, 2015. After that, nothing: no calls, no texts, no banking, no social media, no sign of life of any kind until her body was found on August 8th.

“What person in today’s society, especially a relatively young person, goes without making a cell phone call, making a text, signing onto Wi-Fi, looking at Instagram, checking Facebook? She didn’t touch nothing. Nothing was accessed after that time. She’s dead. And he did it.”

Defense attorney Bob Noel offered a sharply different reading of the same evidence, arguing the state had spent the entire trial trafficking in possibilities rather than proof.

“I’ve never been in a murder case where everything is supposition, guesswork, assumed as this case,” he told Judge Jefferson. “We’re in the proof business, Your Honor, and they haven’t proved anything.”

Noel challenged the timeline Jones had constructed around Katelyn Hearn’s testimony, putting heavy emphasis that Hearn had told police at one point that she heard a thud in Mandy’s bedroom and she thought it could have been between 9 and 9:30 p.m., not around 7:45 as the state suggested, and that she admitted on cross-examination it could have been as late as 8:06 p.m. before she arrived home. He also questioned whether Mandy was even home before her phone connected to a neighbor’s Wi-Fi at 8:13, noting that Facebook Messenger can be accessed from anywhere.

On the four phone calls, Noel suggested a scenario in which Mandy, having just discovered her card was missing, called Chase at the same moment Tellis was calling to access the account. He argued Tellis could have obtained the card any number of ways without ever entering her apartment, and could have seen her PIN when she used her card at Walmart, or she may have had her notebook with her containing the number.

“We have no burden to show how he got it,” Noel said. “They have the burden to prove how he got it.”

The absence of physical evidence was the cornerstone of the defense argument. No DNA belonging to Tellis was found anywhere in Mandy’s apartment. No blood was found in his car despite a Blue Star reagent test. No blood-stained clothing was ever recovered. Noel noted that those facts applied equally to every other person whose DNA was tested, and none of them were charged with murder.

Noel reserved his most pointed attack for Eric Hill, calling him the state’s star witness and arguing the entire murder case collapsed without him. He catalogued Hill’s shifting stories, four by his count, and highlighted what he called the ultimate lie: Hill’s claim to have testified at a prior Tellis trial. No such trial existed, Noel said.

“He has no credibility, Your Honor. Without him, they’ve got nothing but yet they’re guessing.”

Jones countered in rebuttal that Hill had been subpoenaed and present for a preliminary hearing and may have confused the terminology, and that his knowledge of non-public details about Mandy’s injuries was corroboration enough. She pointed out that Tellis had at least 10 days to dispose of any blood evidence between the time when Mandy was killed and when her body was discovered, even before he was first questioned on August 11.

Noel closed by invoking the Jackson v. Virginia standard, arguing that even viewing the evidence in the light most favorable to the state, the prosecution had not proven beyond a reasonable doubt that Quinton Tellis committed this murder.

Jones had the final word in rebuttal, returning to the four phone calls, the missing debit card, the silence that followed July 29th, and the question she said had no reasonable answer.

“There is no one else connected to Mandy and that credit card except for the defendant. There is no one else that was at that apartment with her on July 29th,” she said.

“The biggest tell-all is no electronic footprint after July 29th, 2015. She’s dead. And he did it.”

Judge Larry Jefferson will issue his ruling June 18 at 9 a.m. in Ouachita Parish.

She noted that in six previous calls to Chase in May, Mandy had never once dialed a 1 before the 800 number. She knew she didn’t have to. On July 29th, both calls from her phone included the 1, because, Jones argued, whoever was dialing was reading the number off the back of the debit card, where it is printed with a 1 in front.

“The fact that the four phone calls occurred within the same minute, with the first two being made using Mandy’s cellular phone and the last two being made using the defendant’s cell phone, places Mandy and the defendant together at that point in time without question,” Jones said. “How do we know this? Because on August 8th, when they took all the evidence out of Mandy’s apartment, Mandy’s cell phone was still in the apartment.”

Jones argued that the presence of Mandy’s phone in the apartment on August 8th, combined with its use on the night of July 29th simultaneous with Tellis’s phone, left only one conclusion: he was there. And if he was there and left her alive, Jones said, there was no explaining what came next.

“If he allowed her to live, why in the world would she not immediately pick up the phone and call the police?” Jones said. “Because she was dead. Because he killed her. There is no other reasonable hypothesis.”

Jones addressed the DNA evidence directly, conceding there was none linking Tellis to the scene, but arguing the state of Mandy’s body after 10 days of decomposition in the Louisiana heat would have destroyed whatever was there. She also characterized the Y chromosome found in a rectal swab as not a DNA profile and not evidence of sexual assault, calling it a potential red herring, and noted that 17 people had their DNA tested in connection with the case and none were connected to the scene either.

On the testimony of Eric Hill, Tellis’s wife’s cousin who said Tellis called him from jail and told him to find someone to blame for Mandy’s murder, Jones argued Hill’s knowledge of details that were never made public, including the number and nature of the stab wounds, could only have come from Tellis himself. She acknowledged Hill had told multiple stories but said Detective Duane Cookson’s corroboration of the non-public details was the verification the court needed.

Jones closed by returning to the simplest question in the case. Mandy Hsiao sent a Facebook message at 7:41 p.m. on July 29, 2015. After that, nothing: no calls, no texts, no banking, no social media, no sign of life of any kind until her body was found on August 8th.

“What person in today’s society, especially a relatively young person, goes without making a cell phone call, making a text, signing onto Wi-Fi, looking at Instagram, checking Facebook? She didn’t touch nothing. Nothing was accessed after that time. She’s dead. And he did it.”

Defense attorney Bob Noel offered a sharply different reading of the same evidence, arguing the state had spent the entire trial trafficking in possibilities rather than proof.

“I’ve never been in a murder case where everything is supposition, guesswork, assumed as this case,” he told Judge Jefferson. “We’re in the proof business, Your Honor, and they haven’t proved anything.”

Noel challenged the timeline Jones had constructed around Katelyn Hearn’s testimony, putting heavy emphasis that Hearn had told police at one point that she heard a thud in Mandy’s bedroom and she thought it could have been between 9 and 9:30 p.m., not around 7:45 as the state suggested, and that she admitted on cross-examination it could have been as late as 8:06 p.m. before she arrived home. He also questioned whether Mandy was even home before her phone connected to a neighbor’s Wi-Fi at 8:13, noting that Facebook Messenger can be accessed from anywhere.

On the four phone calls, Noel suggested a scenario in which Mandy, having just discovered her card was missing, called Chase at the same moment Tellis was calling to access the account. He argued Tellis could have obtained the card any number of ways without ever entering her apartment, and could have seen her PIN when she used her card at Walmart, or she may have had her notebook with her containing the number.

“We have no burden to show how he got it,” Noel said. “They have the burden to prove how he got it.”

The absence of physical evidence was the cornerstone of the defense argument. No DNA belonging to Tellis was found anywhere in Mandy’s apartment. No blood was found in his car despite a Blue Star reagent test. No blood-stained clothing was ever recovered. Noel noted that those facts applied equally to every other person whose DNA was tested, and none of them were charged with murder.

Noel reserved his most pointed attack for Eric Hill, calling him the state’s star witness and arguing the entire murder case collapsed without him. He catalogued Hill’s shifting stories, four by his count, and highlighted what he called the ultimate lie: Hill’s claim to have testified at a prior Tellis trial. No such trial existed, Noel said.

“He has no credibility, Your Honor. Without him, they’ve got nothing but yet they’re guessing.”

Jones countered in rebuttal that Hill had been subpoenaed and present for a preliminary hearing and may have confused the terminology, and that his knowledge of non-public details about Mandy’s injuries was corroboration enough. She pointed out that Tellis had at least 10 days to dispose of any blood evidence between the time when Mandy was killed and when her body was discovered, even before he was first questioned on August 11.

Noel closed by invoking the Jackson v. Virginia standard, arguing that even viewing the evidence in the light most favorable to the state, the prosecution had not proven beyond a reasonable doubt that Quinton Tellis committed this murder.

Jones had the final word in rebuttal, returning to the four phone calls, the missing debit card, the silence that followed July 29th, and the question she said had no reasonable answer.

“There is no one else connected to Mandy and that credit card except for the defendant. There is no one else that was at that apartment with her on July 29th,” she said.

“The biggest tell-all is no electronic footprint after July 29th, 2015. She’s dead. And he did it.”

Judge Larry Jefferson will issue his ruling June 18 at 9 a.m. in Ouachita Parish.

item.title: Genuine MS Farmers Market moving to Brandon Amphitheater after strong opening turnout - Darkhorse Press
item.author: Therese Apel
item.description:
BRANDON — The Genuine MS Farmers Market in Brandon is moving to a new location after large crowds during its opening weekend quickly exceeded parking capacity, state officials announced.

Mississippi Agriculture Commissioner Andy Gipson said the seasonal market will begin operating Saturday, May 23, at the Brandon Amphitheater, located at 8190 Rock Way.

Gipson said the decision was made following an “incredibly positive public response” to the market’s debut.

“We are excited to relocate the Genuine MS Farmers Market to the Brandon Amphitheater,” Gipson said in a statement. “This move will also allow the market to grow by adding more vendors as we head into the summer season.”

Brandon Mayor Butch Lee said the city welcomed the move to improve traffic flow and public convenience after the successful opening weekend at the Rankin County Co-op.

“We look forward to seeing everyone there,” Lee said.

Officials said the new location offers better access, additional parking and more room for vendors and shoppers.

The market features vendors selling Mississippi-grown, Mississippi-raised and Mississippi-processed products, including produce, meat, dairy items, honey, plants and specialty foods.

The market is scheduled to operate every Saturday from 8 a.m. until noon through October, weather permitting.

Gipson also thanked the Rankin County Co-op for hosting the market’s opening weekend and said the department hopes to partner with the co-op for future events.

Farmers and producers interested in becoming vendors can contact the Mississippi Department of Agriculture and Commerce at [email protected] or by calling 601-354-6573.

item.title: Flooding closes select clinics at G.V. Sonny Montgomery VA Medical Center - Darkhorse Press
item.author: Morgan Howard
item.description:
JACKSON – Several specialty clinics at the G.V. Sonny Montgomery VA Medical Center were closed Thursday because of flooding.

The closures were announced for the remainder of Thursday, May 21, to ensure the safety of veterans, visitors and staff. Officials said all other clinics, including primary care and other specialty clinic appointments, are continuing as scheduled at this time.

The affected clinics include Women’s Health, also known as the Pink Clinic, Cardiology, Dermatology, Renal, Spinal Cord and Gastroenterology.

Veterans with appointments in those clinics will be contacted directly by staff to move appointments to virtual visits when appropriate or to reschedule for the next available appointment time.

Veterans with appointments outside the affected clinics should continue reporting for care as planned unless they are contacted directly by VA staff.

Anyone with questions about their care or upcoming appointments may contact the Clinical Contact Center at 601-362-4471.

Officials said teams are working to safely address the flooding and restore normal operations.

item.title: DARKHORSE DOGS: Lexington, a gentle Great Dane mix, looking for forever home - Darkhorse Press
item.author: Morgan Howard
item.description:
A gentle giant at the Animal Rescue Fund of Mississippi is looking for a forever home.

Lexington is a neutered Great Dane mix with a gray coat and a calm, loving personality, according to ARF. The rescue said he enjoys getting outside for walks and playtime and is easy to walk.

ARF described Lexington as intelligent, attentive and treat-motivated. He has also spent time in a foster home, where the rescue said he showed how well he bonds with people.

Lexington would do best in a home that understands large-breed dogs and can continue giving him structure and guidance. ARF said he has shown some dog selectivity in the past, so slow and proper introductions to other dogs are important.

The rescue said Lexington can thrive with the right setup and leadership.

Those interested in adopting Lexington can apply online at https://shorturl.at/QfNFQ. ARF’s Amazon wish list is also available at https://shorturl.at/2QMGX.

item.title: Closing arguments set for Thursday in Quinton Tellis murder trial in Louisiana - Darkhorse Press
item.author: Therese Apel
item.description:
MONROE, La. — Closing arguments are scheduled for 1:30 p.m. Thursday in the bench trial of Quinton Tellis, who is charged with the 2015 murder of Monroe woman Mandy Hsiao.

Both the state and defense rested their cases Friday following several days of testimony that included cell phone tower analysis, bank records and witness accounts connecting Tellis to Hsiao’s death and the subsequent use of her bank accounts.

Judge Larry Jefferson will hear closing arguments, though he is not expected to issue a ruling Thursday. No timeline has been given for when a decision is anticipated.

item.title: Jackson police investigating 3 break-ins at Animal Rescue Fund - Darkhorse Press
item.author: Morgan Howard
item.description:
JACKSON – Jackson police are asking for the public’s help after the Animal Rescue Fund of Mississippi was burglarized multiple times in May.

According to the Jackson Police Department, the animal rescue, located at 395 W. Mayes St., was burglarized on May 13, May 19 and May 20. Police said the burglaries happened at different times, but all occurred after 11 p.m.

ARF said the first break-in happened Monday night, when thousands of dollars worth of supplies were stolen from the shelter. According to the organization, the stolen items included a large amount of medicines, vaccines, cleaning products, NexGard Plus for dogs and cats and other supplies. ARF estimated the value of the stolen items to be between $15,000 and $18,000.

ARF said the organization was hit again the next day. During the second burglary, the organization said lawn equipment was stolen, including a large Ryobi lawn mower, a Ryobi weed eater, large Ryobi batteries and a charger.

ARF said a police report was filed, and staff members were gathering camera footage to provide to police.

The organization said the suspect returned again on May 20. During that burglary, ARF said the suspect damaged a fence, broke into a trailer and stole several items, including a recently purchased window unit, ice cream, dog crates used to transport animals for spay and neuter appointments, and copper from a light pole.

The organization said the suspect also damaged security connections and left the trailer with a large opening.

ARF said officers have responded each time to take reports. The organization said police collected items left behind by the suspect and obtained flash drives with video of the thefts.

The suspect is described as a Black male with a slender build and medium complexion. Police said his hair is unknown. Investigators believe the suspect may live in the area where the burglaries occurred.

ARF said the repeated break-ins have caused financial and emotional strain on the rescue, which continues to care for homeless, abandoned, abused, neglected, sick and injured dogs and cats in the community. The organization is asking for donations to help replace stolen supplies, repair damage and continue caring for animals.

Donations may be made through PayPal at [email protected] or mailed to ARF of MS, 395 W. Mayes St., Jackson, MS 39213.

Anyone with information about the burglaries is asked to contact the Jackson Police Department at 601-960-1800 or Crime Stoppers at 601-355-TIPS (8477).

item.author: Therese Apel
item.description:
BYRAM — Two people have been arrested in connection with a shooting Monday in Byram, according to police.

Officers with the Byram Police Department responded to reports of a shooting in the 2200 block of Meagan Drive on May 18. When officers arrived, they found more than 40 shell casings in the roadway and learned that a nearby home had been struck by gunfire.

Authorities said witnesses reported seeing an older model white SUV leave the area at a high rate of speed following the shooting.

Police later arrested one suspect, identified as Micah Harris, on Monday night. Harris is charged with aggravated assault and shooting into an occupied dwelling.

On Tuesday, investigators located the SUV in the 3200 block of Oak Forest Drive in Jackson. A second suspect, identified as Kenneth Kelly Jr., was arrested in connection with the case.

According to police, Kelly was suffering from an untreated gunshot wound and was taken to a local hospital for treatment. He is also charged with shooting into an occupied dwelling.

Authorities said the investigation remains active and ongoing. No additional information has been released.

Anyone with information related to the shooting is asked to contact the Byram Police Department or Central Mississippi Crime Stoppers.

item.title: Travis Howze brings message of hard-fought survival to Mississippi first responders - Darkhorse Press
item.author: Therese Apel
item.description:
(Some adult language)

The internationally known speaker sat down before his keynote address to talk about what it costs to do the job, and what it costs not to deal with that.

FLOWOOD — Travis Howze did three things most people only do one of, if at all: he was a Marine, a police officer and a firefighter. So when he talks about combat, he’s not reaching for a metaphor.

“Our people are in combat every day,” he said Tuesday evening before taking the stage at the 4th Annual Mississippi Public Safety Summit in Flowood. “It’s a different kind of combat, but it’s still combat.”

The difference, he’ll characteristically tell you in colorful terms that might make your mama blush, is one that doesn’t get talked about enough. A soldier goes to a war zone. When the deployment ends, he comes home — and home is not the war zone. The streets where he grew up, the grocery store, the church his kids go to, none of those places are where he lived his worst nightmares. The geography of trauma and the geography of ordinary life stay separate, at least until he goes back.

A first responder never gets that distance.

The neighborhood where a firefighter pulled bodies out of a burning house is the same neighborhood where he coaches Little League on Saturday. The intersection where a cop worked a fatality is on his way to work every morning for the next 30 years. The trauma doesn’t stay in a country on the other side of the world. It’s woven into the place he lives, the roads he drives, the community he raised his family in. Every shift is another layer on top of everything that came before it, and there is no coming home from it because he never left.

Howze, who now travels internationally speaking about mental wellness and trauma recovery, said that accumulation is what most people and most institutions still don’t fully understand about what first responders carry.

“You’re consuming nothing but bad,” he said, “and you’re not offloading it.”

More than 600 law enforcement officers, firefighters, prosecutors and first responders from across Mississippi gathered this week at the Sheraton Flowood The Refuge Hotel and Conference Center for the summit, hosted by the Office of the Attorney General and the Mississippi Department of Public Safety. The event has grown steadily since its 2023 launch, when about 300 attended the inaugural gathering.

Howze was the keynote speaker for opening night.

Facing the fire

Howze says he doesn’t sell recipes.

That’s how he describes what sets him apart from the crowded field of motivational speakers now filling first responder wellness conferences across the country. He doesn’t have it figured out. He just keeps showing up.

“I’m not coming on stage to sell you a recipe that fails me every day,” Howze said Tuesday evening, sitting down for an interview before taking the stage at the 4th Annual Mississippi Public Safety Summit. “Do I have it right? No. Do I knock it out of the park every day? No. But I get up every day and I’m swinging.”

What was missing, then and now

When Howze first started talking publicly about first responder mental health, almost nobody else was doing it the way he was doing it. The national conversation at the time centered almost entirely on military veterans.

“I remember doing the 22 push-ups a day challenges,” he said, referencing the viral awareness campaign for veteran suicide. “I made a whole sold-out 600-seat comedy club do 22 push-ups, and then I remember thinking when I left — did that really do anything other than we did some push-ups together? Did we really move the needle?”

The answer, he came to realize, was incomplete at best. And when he looked around at first responders, he saw people fighting the same battles with almost no spotlight at all.

“Our people are in combat every day. It’s a different kind of combat, but it’s still combat. You still see gnarly stuff, you experience gnarly stuff, and there was nothing for us.”

He’s reluctant to take too much credit for where the conversation has gone since, but he doesn’t entirely back away from it either.

“I don’t like taking the credit for where it is now, but I know I played a large part in it, because at the time when I initially started speaking about this, there was nobody doing first responder wellness from a standpoint of being vulnerable. Nobody. And even with all of the resources we have now, there’s not a lot of people doing that.”

The thing in us that runs toward the nightmare

In June 2007, Howze was a member of the Charleston, South Carolina Fire Department when nine of his brothers, including one of his best friends, were killed in a warehouse fire at a Sofa Super Store. He volunteered for body recovery.

He doesn’t flinch from the question of why, or what it cost him. He said what most young first responders feel — that pull toward the worst of it — comes from a genuinely good place. An idealistic place, he says, but a good one.

“Nobody wants to go to the slow stations. Nobody wants to work in the boring part of towns. Everybody wants to go where it’s busy, and they do that from a naive place, just like I was. I wanted everything that I got. I didn’t realize what came with that.”

He said the problem isn’t the instinct. It’s the failure to reckon with the accumulation.

“We’re running and gunning at a young age. We’re consuming nothing but bad, and we’re not offloading it, we’re not treating ourselves. If we break our leg on duty, we run to the doctor and get it fixed so we can go right back. But when our minds break on duty, we do nothing about it, and we hide from it, and we try to pretend like nothing’s wrong.”

He paused.

item.title: Retired Adams County K-9 Barry remembered for years of service - Darkhorse Press
item.author: Morgan Howard
item.description:
ADAMS COUNTY – The Adams County Sheriff’s Office is mourning the loss of retired K-9 Barry, the agency announced.

Barry was the first dual-purpose K-9 purchased under the current administration at the Adams County Sheriff’s Office, according to the department. He served alongside his handler, Sgt. Thomas McGinty.

During his years of service, Barry assisted in numerous operations, including the recovery of missing persons, the apprehension of fugitives and the seizure of illegal narcotics.

The sheriff’s office said Barry was more than a police dog, describing him as a trusted partner, protector and valued member of the ACSO family.

After Barry’s retirement, McGinty continued to care for him.

“Today, we mourn not just the loss of a K-9, but the loss of a faithful partner and member of our law enforcement family,” the agency said.

The Adams County Sheriff’s Office thanked Barry for his years of dedicated service to Adams County and asked the community to keep McGinty and everyone who loved Barry in their thoughts and prayers.

item.title: Juvenile in Texas in custody after Oxford Middle School bomb threat - Darkhorse Press
item.author: Morgan Howard
item.description:
OXFORD – A juvenile in Texas is in custody after a bomb threat was called in to Oxford Middle School, according to the Oxford Police Department.

Police said the threat was made May 19 through a blocked-number phone call to the school’s front office.

Oxford police school resource officers were already on campus and immediately responded to the threat. The school was placed on lockdown while the first officers on scene worked to make sure students were safe.

Additional officers then set up a perimeter and incident command. Police said the school’s safety plan was activated, and students and staff were evacuated. Students were taken to a reunification site to be reunited with their families.

After the evacuation, officers and K-9 units searched the school room by room to check for any threats inside the building.

Investigators began working to determine the origin of the call and were able to trace the threat to a juvenile in Texas, who is now in custody.

“The safety of the students in our community remains our top priority at the Oxford Police Department,” Chief Jeff McCutchen said. “We are grateful for our relationship with the Oxford School District and their dedication to school safety. This is why it’s so helpful to work together with our school district and other local emergency responders to train these scenarios like we did this past January.”

Police thanked the Oxford School District, Oxford Fire Department, University Police Department, Lafayette County Metro Narcotics Unit, Lafayette County Sheriff’s Department, Mississippi Highway Patrol, Southaven Police Department, Mississippi State University Police Department, DeSoto County Sheriff’s Office, emergency medical services and Oxford police staff for their response.

item.title: Byram police wrangle stray alligator in Branch Creek - Darkhorse Press
item.author: Therese Apel
item.description:
BYRAM — Residents of a quiet Byram neighborhood can rest easier after police say a suspicious suspect with a “light to dark complexion” was taken into custody Wednesday morning following a tense standoff near Branch Creek.

According to the Byram Police Department, officers were dispatched around 5 a.m. after reports of an individual slowly wandering through yards and roadways in the neighborhood.

Witnesses described the suspect as between 4 and 5 feet, moving low to the ground and apparently showing absolutely no regard for traffic laws.

Officers canvassed the area and eventually located what authorities later confirmed was, in fact, an alligator.

“With the assistance of Wildlife & Fisheries, we were able to apprehend the subject,” police said in a statement, adding that citizens could “relax knowing the scaly suspect has been captured.”

Unofficial reports from neighbors claim the reptile resisted arrest briefly before deciding to comply.

No officers were injured during the incident, though the

Officials with the Mississippi Department of Wildlife, Fisheries, and Parks warned that recent heavy rain could lead to more gator sightings near lakes, creeks and rivers across the state.

Authorities reminded residents not to approach alligators. It’s also a bad idea to attempt selfies with them or try to keep them as pets.

item.title: Appeals court upholds denial of parole eligibility for Bolivar County sex offender - Darkhorse Press
item.author: Therese Apel
item.description:
BOLIVAR COUNTY — A Mississippi Court of Appeals panel has affirmed the dismissal of a post-conviction motion filed by a Bolivar County man convicted of child sex crimes, ruling that state law bars him from parole eligibility entirely.

Kendrick Quintarius Gates pleaded guilty in Bolivar County Circuit Court in November 2020 to enticing a child to meet for sexual purposes, enticing a child to produce sexual imagery, and sexual battery. Court records state Gates was 31 at the time of the offenses and the victim was 12 years old. He was sentenced to 40 years in the custody of the Mississippi Department of Corrections on the most serious count, with 15 years suspended, to run concurrently with sentences on the remaining counts.

In November 2023, Gates filed a motion for post-conviction collateral relief, arguing he was being wrongfully denied parole. The circuit court dismissed the motion, finding it was filed after the three-year deadline for post-conviction challenges following a guilty plea. The court also addressed the merits, finding that state law explicitly prohibits Gates from being released on parole.

Gates appealed, arguing his filing was timely under the prison mailbox rule, which provides that an inmate’s motion is considered filed when delivered to prison staff for mailing rather than when received by the court. He also argued that denial of parole violated his constitutional rights under the due process and equal protection clauses of the Fourteenth Amendment.

The Court of Appeals found the timeliness question close enough that the court chose to address his argument on the merits regardless, saying that Gates’s filing appeared to be only days outside the deadline, and a prison mail log submitted separately suggested the motion may have been delivered to staff before the deadline expired.

That argument failed. Judge Kenny Lawrence, writing for the court, cited Mississippi code which prohibits parole for any person sentenced for a sex offense as defined by state law. Gates’s convictions for child enticement and sexual battery fall within that definition, the court found, leaving no legal basis for parole eligibility.

“We are required to follow our Legislature’s enactments,” the court wrote, declining to address Gates’s additional arguments challenging the denial.

The ruling was affirmed Monday. Judge Lawrence was joined by Chief Judge Virginia Carlton Barnes and five other judges in the majority. Three additional judges concurred in part and in the result.

item.title: Texas juvenile arrested after bomb threat prompts lockdown at Oxford Middle School - Darkhorse Press
item.author: Therese Apel
item.description:
OXFORD — A juvenile in Texas is in custody after a bomb threat Tuesday morning prompted a lockdown and evacuation at Oxford Middle School, according to the Oxford Police Department.

Police said officers responded May 19 after the school received a bomb threat through a blocked-number phone call to the front office.

School resource officers immediately secured the campus and placed the school on lockdown while additional officers established a perimeter and incident command, authorities said.

The school district’s safety plan was then activated to evacuate students and staff to a reunification site where students could be picked up by their families.

After the evacuation, officers and K-9 units conducted a room-by-room sweep of the school searching for potential threats inside the building.

Investigators quickly began tracing the source of the call and identified a juvenile in Texas as the suspect. Police said the juvenile is now in custody.

“The safety of the students in our community remains our top priority at the Oxford Police Department,” said Jeff McCutchen. “We are grateful for our relationship with the Oxford School District and their dedication to school safety. This is why it’s so helpful to work together with our school district and other local emergency responders to train these scenarios like we did this past January.”

Oxford police thanked multiple agencies for assisting with the response, including the Oxford Fire Department, University Police Department, Lafayette County Sheriff’s Department, Mississippi Highway Patrol and other regional law enforcement and emergency response agencies.

item.title: Reeves requests major disaster declaration for Mississippi counties hit by severe storms - Darkhorse Press
item.author: Morgan Howard
item.description:
JACKSON – Gov. Tate Reeves has requested a major disaster declaration from President Donald Trump for five Mississippi counties impacted by severe storms earlier this month.

The request covers damage from severe storms, strong tornadoes, straight-line winds, hail and flash flooding that happened May 6-7. According to the governor’s office, the storms produced seven tornadoes, injured 26 people and damaged 425 homes across the state.

“Today, I requested a Major Disaster Declaration from President Trump,” Reeves said. “The state of Mississippi will continue to do everything in its power to help Mississippians rebuild and recover.”

The state is requesting individual assistance for Franklin, Lamar, Lawrence, Lincoln and Wilkinson counties.

FEMA-validated numbers show that in those five counties, 88 homes were destroyed, 112 homes received major damage, 140 had minor damage and 85 homes were affected.

The same five counties are also included in the request for public assistance. Joint damage assessments were conducted by FEMA and the Mississippi Emergency Management Agency, and officials said damage assessments indicate the threshold requirements have been met for public assistance.

According to the governor’s office, the request may be amended in the future to add additional counties if more damage is discovered and reported.

Individual assistance can include grants for temporary housing and home repairs, low-cost loans to cover uninsured property losses and other programs to help people recover from the disaster.

Public assistance helps local governments and certain nonprofits recover from major disasters by providing grant assistance for debris removal, emergency protective measures and the restoration of public infrastructure.

The request must be approved by the president before federal assistance becomes available to local and county governments and certain nonprofits.

item.title: MDWFP reminds boaters of education requirement during National Safe Boating Week - Darkhorse Press
item.author: Morgan Howard
item.description:
JACKSON – The Mississippi Department of Wildlife, Fisheries, and Parks is reminding boaters about the state’s boater education requirement during National Safe Boating Week.

According to MDWFP, anyone born after June 30, 1980, must complete a boater education course before operating a motorized vessel on Mississippi’s public waters.

MDWFP offers both in-person and online boater education courses designed to help boaters understand navigation rules, recognize potential hazards and practice safe boating.

Those who need to complete the course can visit mdwfp.com/enforcement-education/boater-education.

MDWFP said it will share more safe boating tips throughout the week.

item.title: Georgia man arrested in Pontotoc County after major drug seizure on Interstate 22 - Darkhorse Press
item.author: Therese Apel
item.description:
PONTOTOC COUNTY — A Georgia man was arrested Sunday after Mississippi law enforcement officers seized hundreds of pounds of illegal drugs during a commercial vehicle inspection on Interstate 22 in Pontotoc County.

According to the Mississippi Department of Public Safety, the agency’s Interdiction Unit conducted a routine inspection May 17 that resulted in the seizure of approximately 376 pounds of methamphetamine, 82 pounds of marijuana and 2 kilograms of powder cocaine.

Authorities arrested 32-year-old Ramar A. Lloyd of McDonough and transported him to the Pontotoc County Detention Center.

Lloyd is charged with two counts of aggravated trafficking of a controlled substance and one count of trafficking of a controlled substance.

“Mississippi law enforcement remains committed to aggressively targeting drug trafficking operations that threaten the safety of our communities,” said Sean Tindell. “This significant seizure is a direct result of the proactive work being done every day by our law enforcement officers.”

Tindell said dangerous drugs such as methamphetamine and cocaine “destroy lives, fuel violent crime, and have no place in our state.”

The investigation remains ongoing.

item.title: Former Jones County road foreman, contractor plead guilty in embezzlement case - Darkhorse Press
item.author: Morgan Howard
item.description:
JONES COUNTY – A former Jones County road foreman and a contractor have pleaded guilty in connection with a scheme to embezzle county-owned culverts, State Auditor Shad White announced.

According to the State Auditor’s Office, Richard Creel pleaded guilty to one count of embezzlement, and Tommie Landrum pleaded guilty to one count of conspiracy to commit and one count of accessory before the fact.

White’s office said Creel and Landrum were involved in a scheme to embezzle county-owned culverts and transport the property to a predetermined location provided by Landrum.

“The dedicated team at the State Auditor’s office has a zero-tolerance policy for fraud and we will continue to work with prosecutors to get record results for taxpayers,” White said.

Both men were prosecuted in Jones County Circuit Court.

Creel was sentenced to five years of post-release supervision and was ordered to pay $4,925.24 in restitution and $2,927.50 in fines.

Landrum was sentenced to five years, with two years suspended after completion of three years of non-adjudicated probation. He was also ordered to pay $2,462.62 in restitution and $2,927.50 in fines.

Suspected fraud can be reported to the Auditor’s Office by clicking the red button on the office’s website or by calling 1-800-321-1275 during normal business hours.

item.title: Appeals court upholds Natchez man's manslaughter conviction in 2020 shooting - Darkhorse Press
item.author: Therese Apel
item.description:
NATCHEZ — A Mississippi Court of Appeals panel has unanimously upheld the manslaughter conviction of a Natchez man who shot and killed another man in a parking lot dispute in 2020, rejecting all five of his arguments on appeal.

Reginald Tyrone Butler was convicted in Adams County Circuit Court in June 2024 and sentenced to 20 years in the custody of the Mississippi Department of Corrections. The Court of Appeals affirmed that conviction Monday.

According to court records, Butler shot Bralon James on Dec. 17, 2020, at a gathering spot known as the “living room” in Natchez. The shooting followed a confrontation between James and another man over a debt. When that altercation ended, James approached Butler and the two exchanged words before Butler opened fire.

Butler turned himself in to police hours later and claimed self-defense. But the medical examiner determined James died from two gunshot wounds, one to the back and one to the back of the thigh, both fired from more than three to four feet away. Investigators found shell casings only from Butler’s .40-caliber handgun.

At trial, Butler took the stand and denied eight times that he had ever bragged about the killing. The State then played a video in which Butler is heard telling the victim’s brother, “Haha, Braxton. That’s why your brother got shot in the face.” Butler acknowledged appearing in the video.

The jury convicted Butler of manslaughter rather than the charged offense of second-degree murder. He appealed, arguing the video was improperly admitted, that the State used it improperly in closing arguments, that two jury instructions were flawed, and that his trial counsel was ineffective.

The court rejected each argument. On the video, Judge Bradford McCarty, writing for the court, noted that Butler’s trial counsel never objected to its admission or to its use in closing arguments, waiving both issues on appeal. The court also found that Butler had effectively authenticated the video himself by identifying his own appearance in it and offering an explanation for what he said.

On the jury instruction challenges, the court found that Butler’s own defense counsel had requested one of the disputed instructions at trial, barring him from challenging it on appeal. The court also rejected Butler’s claim that the word “unnecessarily” in a second manslaughter instruction was unconstitutionally vague, finding that the term carries a clear common meaning and was further clarified by the self-defense instruction given alongside it.

The court declined to rule on Butler’s ineffective assistance of counsel claim, which alleged his attorney failed to call available witnesses to corroborate his self-defense theory. Such claims are typically reserved for post-conviction proceedings, the court noted, and that avenue remains open to Butler.

The opinion was written by Judge Joel McCarty and joined by all participating judges.
